sd_skylark_man.text: Hear that? A skylark, straight up and singing the whole way. They can keep it going for twenty minutes without a breath you can see.
Meredith wrote a poem about one, and Vaughan Williams set it to music: The Lark Ascending. Every summer it wins a poll. Every summer the lark ignores it.

sd_walker.text: The downs are chalk all the way down: a sea floor, once, made of tiny skeletons. Every footpath up here is white when it rains, and so are your boots.
Fancy a sandwich? I've got cheese and pickle, or pickle and cheese. I'm a rambler, not a caterer.

sd_paraglider_watcher.text: Look down there: the Seven Sisters, all white. Ships used to steer by them. The cliffs are coming towards us at about a foot a year, so I like to visit while there's still a view.

then.text: You met the knucker and lived! And it ate the pie. I'll write it in the parish book: second knucker, first happy ending.
The pie's at the edge of the knucker hole. Come back after dark. Bring a snare, and your manners.
Flour from Jill, a pie dish from the Lanes. Right, stand back.
There. Mutton, onion, a good crust, and no poison, because it's not the 1600s and we've all calmed down.
Leave it by the water and come back at night. Whatever comes up for it, be polite.
Flour from the miller up at Jack and Jill, and a pie dish big enough for a dragon. The antiques shop in Brighton's Lanes has one, I'm told.

else.text: {greeting} That stone in the church is the Slayer's Slab. The tale goes that a dragon, the knucker, lived in that pond and ate the livestock, and the odd person.
A local lad, Jim Pulk some say, baked an enormous poisoned pie, carted it to the pond, and when the knucker ate it, he cut off its head.
I've always felt sorry for the knucker. It lived here first. I'd like to make it up to the family, if there are any.
Help me bake a peace pie? Flour from the miller at Jack and Jill on the Downs, and a pie dish big enough, from the antiques shop in Brighton's Lanes.

then.text: That flour's stone-ground. Wind-ground, really. Jill does the work, I do the sneezing.
A pie for the knucker? Well, that's the strangest order Jill's had since 1852.
Here: a sack of wholemeal, ground this morning. Don't let it get wet. You'll have a pie dish full of glue.

else.text: {greeting} Jill's a post mill: the whole body of the mill turns on one big post to face the wind. You push it round with the tail pole. Some days she pushes back.
Jack's the brick tower one. Only his cap turns. They're a couple, in the way that windmills can be.
The pie sits by the still water. Nothing stirs. Knuckers are night creatures; come back after dark.

then.text: The water heaves. Something long and green and very, very old lifts its head, sniffs the pie, and looks straight at you.
The knucker settles into your snare like it has been waiting for a good excuse. The pie dish is licked clean.

else.text: The knucker slides back into the bottomless dark. The pie is still there. It'll be back.

landsky_knepp.text: {greeting} I volunteer up at Knepp, in the Weald. Three and a half thousand acres of Sussex clay that stopped being a farm in 2001 and started being whatever it wanted.

No ploughs, no sprays. Longhorn cattle, Tamworth pigs, Exmoor ponies and deer wander about and do the work: the pigs turn the soil, the cattle open the scrub, the scrub shelters the songbirds. Nightingales came back. Turtle doves, which have crashed everywhere else. Purple emperor butterflies by the hundred.

In 2020 white storks nested there and raised chicks in the wild, the first in Britain in hundreds of years. Isabella Tree wrote it all up in a book called Wilding. Honest about the mess too: it looks untidy, and people shouted. Nature isn't tidy. Neither are nightingales.

sd_poohsticks.text: It is not Pooh Bridge, which is a way north in Ashdown Forest. But a brook is a brook, and I have a pocket full of sticks.
